questions.q: How is the quantum kernel k(x, x') defined in terms of encoded quantum states |phi(x)> and |phi(x')>?
options: k(x,x') = |<phi(x)|phi(x')>|^2, the squared overlap (fidelity) between the two encoded states
k(x,x') = <phi(x)|phi(x')>, the raw unsquared inner product
k(x,x') is the Euclidean distance between the two classical feature vectors
k(x,x') is always exactly 1 regardless of x and x'
questions.explain: The quantum kernel is defined as the squared overlap (fidelity) between the two encoded quantum states, which always lands between 0 (orthogonal) and 1 (identical), just like a well-behaved classical kernel.

questions.q: Using single-qubit angle encoding, what is k(0.4, 1.2) using k(x,x') = cos^2((x-x')/2)?
options: Approximately 0.8484
Approximately 0.9211
Exactly 1.0
Approximately 0.4
questions.explain: cos((0.4-1.2)/2) = cos(-0.4) is approximately 0.9211, and squaring gives approximately 0.8484 -- confirmed both via the closed-form shortcut and the long-hand inner product calculation, which agree exactly.

questions.q: Why can a quantum kernel be used as a drop-in replacement inside a classical SVM with no changes to the SVM itself?
options: An SVM never needs explicit feature vectors -- it only needs the kernel matrix K[i][j] = k(xi, xj), regardless of whether that matrix was computed classically or via a quantum circuit
Because SVMs are themselves quantum algorithms that require a quantum kernel to function
Because quantum kernels always outperform classical kernels, which is why SVMs are redesigned to use them
Because the quantum kernel and classical RBF kernel produce mathematically identical matrices for any dataset
questions.explain: SVM theory (margins, support vectors, regularization) operates entirely on the kernel matrix K, never on explicit feature vectors -- so swapping in a quantum-computed K changes nothing about how the SVM itself works.

questions.q: What is 'kernel concentration,' and why is it described as a cousin of the barren plateau problem?
options: A failure mode where kernel values cluster near a constant as qubit count grows, losing discriminative power -- structurally similar to how gradients vanish as circuits scale in barren plateaus
A benefit where kernel values become more precise as qubit count grows
A hardware-only effect that has nothing to do with the mathematical structure of the kernel
A guaranteed outcome for every quantum kernel construction, with no exceptions
questions.explain: Some natural quantum kernel constructions have been shown to concentrate -- kernel values become nearly indistinguishable from each other as qubits scale up -- losing the ability to discriminate between data points, echoing the exponential vanishing-signal pattern of barren plateaus.

questions.q: What is the honest state of evidence for quantum kernel methods providing a practical advantage on real-world datasets, per this lesson?
options: No demonstrated case exists where a quantum kernel's SVM beats a well-tuned classical kernel's SVM on real datasets, though specific proven classical-hardness results exist for certain contrived problems
Quantum kernels have been proven to always outperform classical RBF kernels on real-world data
Quantum kernel methods are purely theoretical and cannot be computed even in simulation
Quantum kernel methods have been completely abandoned by researchers due to proven failure
questions.explain: Consistent with the course's overall honest framing, proven classical-hardness results exist for specially constructed problems, but no real-world dataset has shown a quantum kernel SVM beating a well-tuned classical kernel SVM in practice.
